EVEWorld: Physical Evolution Supervision for Embodied World Models

Kaiqi Wang Affiliation: China Merchants Group    Songxin Zhang Affiliation: China Merchants Group    Zejian Xie Affiliation: China Merchants Group    Xiao Xiong Affiliation: China Merchants Group    Zhuoyang Song Affiliation: China Merchants Group    Ziwei Wu Affiliation: China Merchants Group    Jun Yu Lu Affiliation: China Merchants Group    Yitan Teng Affiliation: China Merchants Group    Ziying Song Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University Affiliation: Corresponding authors: Ziying Song (ziying.song@ntu.edu.sg), Jiaxing Zhang (zhangjiaxing@cmhk.com)     Jiaxing Zhang Affiliation: China Merchants Group Affiliation: Corresponding authors: Ziying Song (ziying.song@ntu.edu.sg), Jiaxing Zhang (zhangjiaxing@cmhk.com) 
Abstract

Embodied world models enable scalable simulation of embodied interactions for robot learning. However, existing models are prone to Model Laziness, as they focus on visual fidelity at the expense of physical reasoning and lack process-level supervision over the temporal dynamics of manipulated objects. In this work, we propose EVEWorld, a physical evolution-supervision framework for physically consistent target evolution. EVEWorld consists of two components: Instance-Guided Restoration (IGR) and Temporal Instance Alignment (TIA). First, IGR promotes instance consistency through restoration supervision. Second, TIA promotes cross-frame consistency by aligning target instances across adjacent frames. We further introduce the Model Laziness Rate (MLR), a metric that measures persistent violations of instance consistency in generated trajectories. Extensive experiments on DreamGenBench, EWMBench, and PBench demonstrate the effectiveness of EVEWorld, notably achieving an 87.5% reduction in MLR compared with GigaWorld-0. On the WorldArena 2.0 Track 1 leaderboard, our model ranks 6th in JEPA Similarity and 17th overall, which further validates the performance of our evolution supervision strategy.

https://behappya.github.io/EVEWorld/

1 Introduction

Embodied world models and related policy-learning methods are emerging as scalable predictive engines for embodied intelligence, modeling diverse interaction dynamics to support robot learning, planning, and simulation (Yang et al., 2024a; Bruce et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Jang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b; Du et al., 2023; Schmidt & Jiang, 2024; Ye et al., 2025; Zitkovich et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025; Black et al., 2025; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025). Recent work (Huang et al., 2025a; Huang et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026; GigaWorld Team et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2025a; Pang et al., 2025; Dou et al., 2026; Duan et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026; Bardhan et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025c; Li et al., 2026; Quevedo et al., 2026) has further advanced embodied world modeling and its evaluation through high-fidelity generation, multiview and long-context modeling, action conditioning, persistent memory, and task-oriented evaluation.

Recent embodied world models further strengthen structural faithfulness through explicit 4D RGB–depth–normal prediction, geometry-aware action conditioning, and disentangled dynamics and visual synthesis, with related physical-evaluation benchmarks (Zhen et al., 2025; DreamX Team et al., 2026; Shan et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025a; Bansal et al., 2026; Meng et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2025; Shang et al., 2026a; Motamed et al., 2026; Garrido et al., 2025). Nevertheless, stronger visual and structural modeling does not necessarily ensure physically consistent target evolution: a rollout may exhibit target-instance consistency failures, such as duplication or disappearance, and cross-frame consistency failures, such as deformation and identity drift (Yuan et al., 2026; Foo et al., 2026). Figure 1 shows a representative instance consistency failure after standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We refer to such instance consistency failures as Model Laziness: frame-level reconstruction can admit a shortcut that satisfies appearance or endpoint cues without maintaining instance consistency throughout the interaction.

In this work, we propose EVEWorld, an evolution-supervision framework that promotes physically consistent target evolution and mitigates Model Laziness in embodied world models, as shown in Figure 2. EVEWorld comprises two complementary components: Instance-Guided Restoration (IGR), which promotes instance consistency by restoring count-perturbed videos, and Temporal Instance Alignment (TIA), which promotes cross-frame consistency by aligning target instances across adjacent frames. To quantify Model Laziness, we introduce the Model Laziness Rate (MLR), a metric that measures persistent violations of target-instance consistency over a rollout. Extensive evaluations on DreamGenBench, WorldArena 2.0, EWMBench, and PBench demonstrate the effectiveness of EVEWorld in promoting physically consistent target evolution. Notably, on the WorldArena 2.0 Track 1 leaderboard, EVEWorld achieves an EWMScore-P of 70.17, ranking 17th overall and 6th in JEPA Similarity. These results further support the effectiveness of evolution supervision under large-scale world-model evaluation.

2 Related Work

Video Generation Models for Robotics.

Large-scale video models provide strong priors for embodied prediction and scalable robot-data generation (Blattmann et al., 2023; Brooks et al., 2024; Team Wan et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2024), enabling world models for robot learning, planning, and simulation (Yang et al., 2024a; Zhou et al., 2024; Jang et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2025; GigaWorld Team et al., 2025). Recent work (Zhen et al., 2025; DreamX Team et al., 2026; Shan et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2026) further strengthens structural modeling through richer representations and conditioning: TesserAct jointly predicts RGB, depth, and normals, DreamX-Phi incorporates geometric action conditioning and depth supervision, and DVG-WM disentangles dynamics from visual synthesis, and RoboMaster improves multi-object interaction modeling. In contrast, our EVEWorld retains the host model’s native representation and introduces evolution supervision during post-training to promote physically consistent target evolution.

Physical Reasoning in Embodied World Models.

Prior works (Yang et al., 2024b; Traub et al., 2024; Jeong et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2025a; Dou et al., 2026) improve object-centric and temporally consistent modeling through correspondence, tracking, object permanence, and persistent memory, while other studies (Deng et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2025; Khose et al., 2026) examine object dynamics, quantity behavior, and broader aspects of physical reasoning from different perspectives. However, despite these advances and evaluations (Yang et al., 2024b; Traub et al., 2024; Jeong et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2025a; Dou et al., 2026; Deng et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2025; Khose et al., 2026), physically consistent target evolution remains challenging, with manipulated objects exhibiting failures in both instance consistency and cross-frame consistency. In contrast, our EVEWorld introduces evolution supervision to explicitly promote physically consistent target evolution.

3 Why Embodied World Models Become Lazy

3.1 Problem Statement

Given an initial observation I0I_{0} and an instruction cc, an embodied video world model predicts future frames x1:Tx_{1:T}. We focus on manipulation scenarios that require instance consistency, where the target-instance count is expected to remain unchanged throughout the interaction.

Let Nt​(I0,xt,c)N_{t}(I_{0},x_{t},c) denote the number of instances of the target specified by cc, with N0​(I0,c)N_{0}(I_{0},c) denoting its initial count. We define Model Laziness as

ML(I0,x1:T,c)=𝕀[∃t∈{1,…,T}:Nt(I0,xt,c)≠N0(I0,c)].\mathrm{ML}(I_{0},x_{1:T},c)=\mathbb{I}\!\left[\exists t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}:N_{t}(I_{0},x_{t},c)\neq N_{0}(I_{0},c)\right]. (1)

This captures instance consistency failures caused by unsupported target duplication or disappearance. Interactions that intentionally change the target-instance count, such as cutting or assembly, are outside the scope of the current formulation and MLR protocol. Robot-induced occlusion is handled separately through an occlusion-aware check during MLR evaluation.

3.2 Causes of Model Laziness

Standard training emphasizes visual reconstruction while providing limited process-level supervision for physically consistent target evolution (Denton & Fergus, 2018; Bengio et al., 2015; Jeong et al., 2025). This leaves two key gaps: instance consistency and cross-frame consistency.

Missing Instance-Consistency Supervision. Experimental results show that Standard SFT retains 92%–99% of the injected target area across different perturbation settings (Appendix Figure 10, Appendix C.2). Because the perturbed region is small relative to the full frame, its reconstruction error can be diluted by the surrounding scene, providing insufficient supervision for recovering the correct target-instance count. IGR (Section 4.1) addresses this gap by providing a direct restoration target and assigning greater spatial weight to the perturbed region.

Missing Cross-frame Consistency Supervision. IGR improves instance consistency, but a correct target-instance count alone does not ensure cross-frame consistency; the target may still become distorted, fade, or shift abruptly across adjacent frames, as shown in Figure 2(b). This stems from the lack of explicit supervision linking the same target across frames, allowing locally plausible predictions to evolve inconsistently over time. TIA (Section 4.2) addresses this gap by aligning target instances across adjacent frames.

4 Method

Framework Overview.

Given a clean demonstration video xx and its instruction cc, EVEWorld uses IGR (Section 4.1) to construct a count-edited video x~\tilde{x} and trains the model to restore xx, assigning higher weights to restoration-related regions to promote instance consistency. TIA (Section 4.2) operates within the video diffusion transformer to align target features across adjacent frames and promote cross-frame consistency. Together, IGR and TIA enable physically consistent target evolution in the final video output. Notably, the demonstration video is used for training supervision; at inference, EVEWorld takes only the initial image and instruction as input.

4.1 Instance-Guided Restoration

To address failures in physically consistent target evolution, we introduce Instance-Guided Restoration (IGR) to promote instance consistency. IGR inserts an extra target instance into clean demonstrations to form count-edited samples, then trains the model to restore the corresponding clean latent representation encoded by a pretrained VAE. A language model and GroundingDINO (Liu et al., 2024a) localize the target trajectory to sample a target patch pp and valid paste region Ω\Omega:

x~=Paste⁡(x,p,Ω),z=VAE⁡(x),z~=VAE⁡(x~).\tilde{x}=\mathrm{Paste}(x,p,\Omega),\qquad z=\mathrm{VAE}(x),\qquad\tilde{z}=\mathrm{VAE}(\tilde{x}). (2)

Training the model to map the count-edited latent z~\tilde{z} back to the clean latent zz encourages recovery of the correct target-instance count. To prevent this local instance-consistency signal from being diluted by global reconstruction, we assign restoration-related regions three times the reconstruction weight of ordinary regions and normalize the resulting spatial weight map to unit mean. We denote the normalized map by W^\hat{W}; its exact construction is given in Appendix B.1. Using the EDM-style noise weighting λ⁡(σ)\lambda(\sigma) (Karras et al., 2022), the restoration objective is

ℒIGR=𝔼⁡[λ⁡(σ)​1C​T​H​W​|W^1/2⊙(Dθ​(z~+σ​ϵ,c,σ)−z)|22].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IGR}}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lambda(\sigma)\frac{1}{CTHW}\left|\hat{W}^{1/2}\odot\left(D_{\theta}(\tilde{z}+\sigma\epsilon,c,\sigma)-z\right)\right|_{2}^{2}\right]. (3)

Minimizing ℒIGR\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IGR}} provides explicit instance-consistency supervision by recovering the correct target-instance state from count-perturbed inputs; details are provided in Appendix B.1.

4.2 Temporal Instance Alignment

IGR improves instance consistency, but a correct target-instance count alone does not guarantee cross-frame consistency. Failures such as identity drift, distortion, fading, or abrupt motion may still occur across adjacent frames. We therefore introduce Temporal Instance Alignment (TIA) to explicitly promote cross-frame consistency by aligning target instances across adjacent frames.

We select the attachment layer using an offline layer-wise matching probe. For each candidate layer ℓ\ell, the frame-(t−1)(t-1) target feature retrieves its best match over all token cells of frame tt, and we select the layer with the lowest endpoint error (EPE):

u^tℓ=arg⁡maxv​ft−1ℓ​(ut−1)⊤​ftℓ​(v),ℓ⋆=arg⁡minℓ∈ℬ​1|𝒱|​∑t∈𝒱‖u^tℓ−ut‖2.\hat{u}_{t}^{\ell}=\arg\max_{v}f_{t-1}^{\ell}(u_{t-1})^{\top}f_{t}^{\ell}(v),\qquad\ell^{\star}=\arg\min_{\ell\in\mathcal{B}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{V}}\left\|\hat{u}_{t}^{\ell}-u_{t}\right\|_{2}. (4)

where 𝒱\mathcal{V} contains adjacent-frame pairs with the target visible in both frames and detector confidence above a threshold. At layer ℓ⋆\ell^{\star}, TIA has two stages (Figure 3, right). Local instance locating matches target features within a local neighborhood, while cross-frame instance transport converts pre-transport cosine similarities into softmax transport weights, splats projected previous-frame features into frame tt, normalizes by transport mass, and writes them back through a zero-initialized bounded residual.

Ht′=Htℓ⋆+γ​tanh⁡(Wout​(H¯t−Win​Htℓ⋆)).H_{t}^{\prime}=H_{t}^{\ell^{\star}}+\gamma\,\tanh\!\left(W_{\mathrm{out}}\big(\bar{H}_{t}-W_{\mathrm{in}}H_{t}^{\ell^{\star}}\big)\right). (5)

Here, H¯t\bar{H}_{t} denotes the transported feature field. GroundingDINO and target locations utu_{t} provide offline alignment supervision during training only; at inference, dense matching and transport operate directly on the model’s hidden features and require neither target localization nor an external tracker. The transported features are further supervised to favor the true next-frame target location over nearby candidates:

ℒTIA=−1|𝒱|∑t∈𝒱logexp⁡(st,ut/τ)∑v∈𝒞texp⁡(st,v/τ),st,v=f¯t−1ℓ⋆(ut−1)⊤f¯tℓ⋆(v),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TIA}}=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{V}}\log\frac{\exp(s_{t,u_{t}}/\tau)}{\sum_{v\in\mathcal{C}_{t}}\exp(s_{t,v}/\tau)},\qquad s_{t,v}=\bar{f}_{t-1}^{\ell^{\star}}(u_{t-1})^{\top}\bar{f}_{t}^{\ell^{\star}}(v), (6)

where f¯ℓ⋆\bar{f}^{\ell^{\star}} is the normalized feature after transport. The locating, transport, and alignment components jointly constrain target identity across frames. Further details are provided in Appendix B.2.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup and Metrics

Benchmarks and Data Splits.

We use the official DreamGen GR1 fine-tuning split, which contains 92 robot-manipulation videos paired with instructions, and primarily evaluate on DreamGenBench, comprising 126 manipulation tasks across unseen environments, objects, and behaviors (Jang et al., 2025). We further evaluate cross-domain generalization on WorldArena 1.0, cross-trial robustness on PBench, cross-distribution generalization on AgiBot–EWMBench, and cross-backbone generalization using FlowWAM on WorldArena 2.0 and held-out RoboTwin actions (Shang et al., 2026a; Shang et al., 2026b; AgiBot-World-Contributors et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025; Mu et al., 2025; NVIDIA, 2025b; Huang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024b; Unterthiner et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2026a).

Evaluation Metrics.

We evaluate instruction following with Qwen-IF and Gemini-IF (Bai et al., 2025; Gemini Team et al., 2023); WorldArena 1.0/2.0, EWMBench, PBench, and RoboTwin assess complementary aspects of perceptual quality, motion, semantics, consistency, and task fidelity.

Related evaluations (Deng et al., 2026; Khose et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2025), including RBench, WFM-Eval, and video numeracy benchmarks, provide indirect signals related to object quantity and persistence. In contrast, we propose the Model Laziness Rate (MLR), a metric that explicitly measures target-instance consistency at the rollout level using the observed initial count N0N_{0} as its reference, without requiring a prompt-specified count or reference future. We exclude under-counts attributable to robot-induced occlusion while retaining all over-counts, and denote the resulting evaluation count by N~t​(x)\widetilde{N}_{t}(x). MLR implements Eq. 1 with a two-frame persistence criterion to suppress isolated detection errors. We define

MLR=100|𝒟+|∑x∈𝒟+𝕀[∃t∈{1,…,T−1}:N~t(x)≠N0(x)∧N~t+1(x)≠N0(x)],\mathrm{MLR}=\frac{100}{|\mathcal{D}_{+}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{+}}\mathbb{I}\!\left[\exists t\in\{1,\ldots,T-1\}:\widetilde{N}_{t}(x)\neq N_{0}(x)\land\widetilde{N}_{t+1}(x)\neq N_{0}(x)\right], (7)

where 𝒟+={x∈𝒟:N0​(x)>0}\mathcal{D}_{+}=\{x\in\mathcal{D}:N_{0}(x)>0\}. Further details are provided in Appendix A.

Model and Training Setup.

For the main experiments, we initialize EVEWorld from the 2B-parameter GigaWorld-0 Video-Pretrain-2B (GigaWorld Team et al., 2025) and compare against CogVideoX1.5, Wan2.2, and Cosmos-Predict2 as zero-shot baselines (Yang et al., 2025; Team Wan et al., 2025; NVIDIA, 2025a). Standard SFT, EVEWorld, and all ablations share the same initialization, training data, and 250-step optimization budget. We fine-tune all transformer parameters on eight NVIDIA H20Z GPUs with an effective batch size of 64 and a learning rate of 4.32×10−54.32\times 10^{-5}. For cross-distribution and cross-backbone experiments, we apply the same evolution-supervision method to the corresponding data and backbone. Details are provided in the appendix.

5.2 Main Results

Overall Results.

As shown in Table 1, EVEWorld substantially mitigates Model Laziness while improving instruction following. Compared with Standard SFT, EVEWorld reduces MLR from 11.11% to 1.59% (85.7% relative reduction), while Qwen-IF increases from 73.81% to 80.16% and Gemini-IF from 53.57% to 60.85%. Appendix A (Appendix Figure 8) further shows that the remaining violations under EVEWorld are transient, indicating that evolution supervision improves physical consistency without sacrificing instruction following.

Fine-grained Analysis.

Table 2 reports instruction-following performance across the Environment, Object, and Behavior splits. Compared with Standard SFT, EVEWorld improves Qwen-IF on all three splits, with the largest gain on Behavior (68.09% to 76.60%), while Gemini-IF improves notably on Environment (51.72% to 72.41%) and Object (42.00% to 50.33%). Overall, these results show that evolution supervision yields broad gains across different generalization dimensions.

5.3 Generalization Evaluation

Zero-Shot Domain Generalization.

On WorldArena 1.0 (Shang et al., 2026a), which includes unseen scenes and robot embodiments, EVEWorld improves EWMScore-local-8 from 53.95 to 56.76 (+5.21%) over Standard SFT while reducing MLR from 27.39% to 13.38% (−-51.15%) (Table 3). These results demonstrate improved cross-domain generalization in both motion quality and target-instance consistency.

Generalization Across Training Distributions.

On EWMBench (Hu et al., 2025), EVEWorld trained on the same AgiBot data (AgiBot-World-Contributors et al., 2025) and optimization budget as Standard SFT improves Motion and Overall by 3.48% and 1.24%, respectively (Table 4). These results show that the gains of EVEWorld extend beyond the DreamGen training distribution, particularly in motion modeling.

Cross-Backbone Generalization.

We replace the GigaWorld image-text-conditioned IT2V backbone with FlowWAM’s flow-conditioned WAM architecture (Table 5). On FlowWAM, IGR improves all reported metrics over Standard SFT on held-out RoboTwin actions, but TIA yields consistently larger gains. The full model continues to outperform Standard SFT, suggesting that the contributions of IGR and TIA are backbone-dependent. The resulting FlowWAM-based EVEWorld model, SupervisionWM, achieves an EWMScore-P of 70.17 on the official WorldArena 2.0 Track 1 leaderboard, ranking 17th overall and 6th in JEPA Similarity. These results support the cross-backbone generalization of our evolution-supervision framework, while the optimal component configuration may depend on the model architecture.

5.4 Ablation Studies and Analysis

Component Contributions of IGR and TIA.

Table 6 shows that IGR primarily improves instance consistency, reducing MLR from 11.11% to 4.76%; TIA improves cross-frame consistency and Overall Gemini-IF. Combining both yields 1.59% MLR and a Gemini-IF score of 60.85, demonstrating complementary effects under the GigaWorld-0 image-text-conditioned IT2V architecture.

Cross-Trial Robustness.

We further evaluate EVEWorld on PBench Robot across multiple stochastic inference trials under a matched-budget setting, with evolution supervision as the only methodological difference from SFT250. As shown in Table 8, EVEWorld improves all six paired trials across 3.8 s and 5.8 s rollouts, with mean gains of +1.54+1.54 and +1.56+1.56, respectively, demonstrating consistent robustness across inference seeds and rollout horizons.

Exploration of Alternative Approaches.

We explored five alternative approaches to mitigate Model Laziness while improving instruction fidelity: PhysicsLatent, EAG, LAD-LoRA, Causal Frontier, and ICH-D (Table 7). However, none achieved both objectives simultaneously. For example, PhysicsLatent reduces Model Laziness at an 11.9% cost in instruction fidelity, whereas EAG gains 10.0% in instruction fidelity at a 150.0% increase in Model Laziness. We share these trade-offs to provide practical insights for future research, with further details in Appendix D.

CFG Sensitivity Analysis.

Figure 4 shows that Gemini-IF generally increases with higher CFG weights, but MLR varies non-monotonically across guidance weights and training stages. Thus, CFG does not reliably improve instruction fidelity and reduce Model Laziness simultaneously, indicating the importance of explicit supervision for target evolution.

Sequence-Length Scaling and Inference Cost.

Table 9 shows that increasing output duration from 3.8 to 19.8 s raises p50/p95 latency from 8.17/8.40 to 41.74/45.01 s and GPU-hour cost per 1,000 videos from 18.40 to 95.34, with relatively stable throughput and peak memory. Thus, longer rollouts mainly increase computation with limited additional memory overhead.

6 Conclusion

We presented EVEWorld, a physical evolution supervision framework for embodied world models, and proposed the Model Laziness Rate (MLR), a metric to quantify target-instance consistency failures, which we term Model Laziness. EVEWorld combines IGR for instance consistency and TIA for cross-frame consistency to promote physically consistent target evolution. Experiments show an 85.7% MLR reduction on DreamGenBench with improved instruction following, 17th overall and 6th in JEPA Similarity on the WorldArena 2.0 Track 1 leaderboard, and generalization gains across training distributions and model backbones.

Limitations and Future Works.

The limitations of our current formulation mainly arise from its local, pairwise supervision, which does not explicitly capture long-horizon state dependencies or complex multi-object interactions. Future work will further expand the EVEWorld framework with broader forms of evolution supervision for longer-horizon and relational dynamics.

Reproducibility Statement

The appendices document the training and evaluation settings. The supplementary material and the public repository provide code, data indices, configurations, evaluation prompts, and item-level results. The repository is available at https://github.com/behappya/EVEWorld.

The AI tools were not used for developing the method, conducting experiments, generating results, or making scientific decisions. Appendix A Model Laziness and MLR

MLR detects persistent deviations from the initial target-instance count N0N_{0}, while under-counts supported by robot-induced occlusion are exempted and all over-counts are retained. Appendix C.2 tests recovery from an injected count error. Appendix A.1 details the evaluation protocol and occlusion check; Appendices A.4–A.5 cover model, detector, and domain variation.

A.1 MLR: Comparison with Existing Evaluation Metrics

Existing evaluations expose signals related to object persistence and quantity, but differ in both their evaluation anchors and aggregation units.

RBench. RBench evaluates spontaneous entity emergence and disappearance as part of Physical-Semantic Plausibility (PSS), together with other physical-semantic violations such as floating, penetration, and non-contact attachment (Deng et al., 2026). After normalization, PSS is combined with Task-Adherence Consistency (TAC) into the Task Completion score:

TCRBench=PSS+TAC2.\mathrm{TC}_{\mathrm{RBench}}=\frac{\mathrm{PSS}+\mathrm{TAC}}{2}. (8)

Thus, appearance and disappearance failures contribute to a broader assessment of physical plausibility and task correctness rather than forming an independent rollout-level target-instance consistency metric. In contrast, MLR isolates target-instance consistency as a dedicated evaluation unit, making instance-consistency failures directly measurable rather than subsuming them into a broader composite score.

WFM-Eval. WFM-Eval explicitly diagnoses object hallucination and temporal inconsistency by comparing a generated video V^\hat{V} with a ground-truth reference video V∗V^{\ast} (Khose et al., 2026). It distinguishes phantom appearance, phantom disappearance, position drift, and frame jump. Let npan_{\mathrm{pa}}, npdn_{\mathrm{pd}}, ndrn_{\mathrm{dr}}, and njpn_{\mathrm{jp}} denote the numbers of these detected events over MM generated frames and KK tracked objects. Its Object Hallucination Rate (OHR) and Harm-weighted Severity Score (HSS) are

OHRWFM=npa+npdM,HSSWFM=min⁡(1,∑e∈ℰw⁡(e)M​K),\mathrm{OHR}_{\mathrm{WFM}}=\frac{n_{\mathrm{pa}}+n_{\mathrm{pd}}}{M},\qquad\mathrm{HSS}_{\mathrm{WFM}}=\min\!\left(1,\frac{\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}}w(e)}{MK}\right), (9)

where w⁡(e)w(e) assigns event-dependent severity weights. These metrics provide fine-grained reference-grounded diagnostics. MLR instead anchors evaluation to the observed initial target state and therefore requires no ground-truth future, enabling target-instance consistency to be evaluated when only the conditioning observation and generated rollout are available.

T2V-CompBench. Generative numeracy in T2V-CompBench is prompt-anchored (Sun et al., 2025). GroundingDINO counts each prompted object class in every evaluated frame; a class receives score 1 if the detected quantity matches the quantity specified in the text prompt and 0 otherwise. The frame score averages over object classes, and the video score averages over frames. This rule can be written as

Snum=1T∑t=1T1J∑j=1J𝕀[n^t,j=njprompt],S_{\mathrm{num}}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^{J}\mathbb{I}\!\left[\hat{n}_{t,j}=n^{\mathrm{prompt}}_{j}\right], (10)

where n^t,j\hat{n}_{t,j} is the detected count of object class jj at frame tt, njpromptn^{\mathrm{prompt}}_{j} is its prompt-specified quantity, and JJ is the number of queried object classes. This metric therefore evaluates frame-wise agreement with prompt-specified quantities rather than target-instance consistency with the observed target population throughout an interaction. MLR instead derives the expected target count from the conditioning observation itself, allowing target-instance consistency to be evaluated even when the instruction does not explicitly specify a quantity.

RoboWM-Bench. RoboWM-Bench evaluates a different property: embodied executability (Jiang et al., 2026). Predicted human-hand or robotic videos are converted into executable actions through human-centric retargeting or a robot-centric inverse dynamics model (IDM), respectively, and the resulting actions are executed in simulation. Evaluation combines step-level checks at semantically meaningful action nodes with final task-level success. If CrC_{r} denotes whether key action node rr satisfies its required interaction and dynamical constraints and GG denotes achievement of the final task objective, its stated task-success criterion can be summarized as

Stask=𝕀⁡[(⋀r=1RCr)∧G].S_{\mathrm{task}}=\mathbb{I}\!\left[\left(\bigwedge_{r=1}^{R}C_{r}\right)\land G\right]. (11)

This protocol measures whether generated behavior can be translated into successful embodied execution rather than directly measuring target-instance consistency in the generated rollout. MLR provides a complementary model-side diagnostic by directly identifying persistent target-count violations in the generated video, without requiring action decoding or simulator execution.

Positioning and Design Advantages of MLR.

Taken together, these evaluations address complementary aspects of video and embodied-world-model quality but rely on different evaluation anchors. RBench embeds appearance and disappearance within broader physical and task-level assessment; WFM-Eval evaluates hallucination events relative to a ground-truth future; T2V-CompBench evaluates quantities explicitly specified by the prompt; and RoboWM-Bench assesses downstream embodied execution. MLR is designed for the complementary regime in which the conditioning observation itself defines the expected target count and no reference future is assumed. It therefore provides four properties that are particularly useful for embodied manipulation evaluation: it is initial-state anchored, because the observed initial target count N0N_{0} is obtained directly from the conditioning state; reference-free, because no ground-truth future is required; rollout-level and persistence-aware, because sustained violations are distinguished from isolated frame-level fluctuations; and occlusion-aware, because robot-supported under-counts are explicitly exempted. Together, these properties make MLR a dedicated diagnostic for persistent target-instance consistency failures in embodied world-model rollouts.

We operationalize MLR as follows. For DreamGenBench, eligibility is determined once from the fixed conditioning frame with GroundingDINO (Liu et al., 2024a) and the same target query, yielding the shared set 𝒰63\mathcal{U}_{63} used for every model. GroundingDINO then counts target instances at TT uniformly sampled future timestamps in each generated video. Spatially redundant detections are merged; items with no detectable target in the conditioning frame are excluded from the shared set. We denote the eligible set by

𝒟+={x∈𝒟:N0​(x)>0}.\mathcal{D}_{+}=\{x\in\mathcal{D}:N_{0}(x)>0\}.

We first identify deviations from the initial target-instance count N0N_{0}. Over-counts, i.e., Nt>N0N_{t}>N_{0}, are always retained as duplication evidence. For under-counts, i.e., Nt<N0N_{t}<N_{0}, we further check whether the missing target is supported by robot-induced occlusion.

SAM2 (Ravi et al., 2025) tracks each target instance across the rollout. When the current target mask of an instance is unavailable, we use its most recent reliable mask as the reference target region. GroundingDINO localizes the robot in the current frame, and SAM2 converts the detected robot boxes into an occluder mask MtrobotM_{t}^{\mathrm{robot}}. For each missing target instance ii, we compute the target–robot overlap ratio

ri,tocc=|M^i,ttarget∩Mtrobot||M^i,ttarget|,r^{\mathrm{occ}}_{i,t}=\frac{\left|\widehat{M}^{\mathrm{target}}_{i,t}\cap M_{t}^{\mathrm{robot}}\right|}{\left|\widehat{M}^{\mathrm{target}}_{i,t}\right|}, (12)

where M^i,ttarget\widehat{M}^{\mathrm{target}}_{i,t} denotes the reliable target reference region used for the occlusion check.

Motivated by prior amodal-segmentation criteria (Xiao et al., 2021; Zeng et al., 2022; Zhan et al., 2024) and target-normalized occlusion reasoning in robotic manipulation (Wada et al., 2018), we set τocc=0.15\tau_{\mathrm{occ}}=0.15 and treat an under-count as occlusion-supported only if ri,tocc≥τoccr^{\mathrm{occ}}_{i,t}\geq\tau_{\mathrm{occ}} for every missing target instance; Appendix A.3 confirms that the comparison is robust to nearby thresholds. Such under-counts are excluded from violation evidence, whereas all other under-counts and all over-counts are retained. Let ot​(x)=1o_{t}(x)=1 indicate an occlusion-supported under-count. We define the resulting evaluation count as

N~t​(x)={N0​(x),ot​(x)=1,Nt​(x),otherwise.\widetilde{N}_{t}(x)=\begin{cases}N_{0}(x),&o_{t}(x)=1,\\ N_{t}(x),&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (13)

For each eligible video, an MLR event is recorded when the adjusted count deviates from N0N_{0} at two consecutive sampled timestamps:

e⁡(x)\displaystyle e(x) =𝕀[∃t∈{1,…,T−1}:N~t(x)≠N0(x)∧N~t+1(x)≠N0(x)],\displaystyle=\mathbb{I}\!\left[\exists t\in\{1,\ldots,T-1\}:\widetilde{N}_{t}(x)\neq N_{0}(x)\land\widetilde{N}_{t+1}(x)\neq N_{0}(x)\right],
MLR\displaystyle\mathrm{MLR} =100|𝒟+|​∑x∈𝒟+e⁡(x).\displaystyle=\frac{100}{|\mathcal{D}_{+}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{+}}e(x). (14)

Unlike frame-wise count agreement, MLR records a violation only when the inconsistency persists at the rollout level. An occlusion-supported under-count resets the persistence criterion, whereas a target that remains missing after the robot occluder moves away again provides disappearance evidence. Requiring two consecutive violating timestamps suppresses isolated detector errors while retaining sustained duplication and disappearance as consistency failures. All detector, query, occlusion-threshold, and persistence settings are fixed across models.

Beyond the scalar MLR value, the same event definition localizes each violation in time. For an MLR-positive rollout, we record the first persistent violation as its onset and analyze how long the count deviation persists. These diagnostics distinguish short detector fluctuations from sustained consistency failures and enable direct inspection of the corresponding generated segment.

Occlusion example.

Figure 5 illustrates how the occlusion check distinguishes temporary robot occlusion from target disappearance. During sufficient robot–target overlap, a missing target is excluded from violation evidence. Once the robot moves away, a target that remains missing is again treated as an under-count and contributes to an MLR event if the deviation persists across consecutive sampled timestamps.

A.2 Scope and Limitations of MLR

MLR is designed for manipulation scenarios that require instance consistency, including grasping, transport, placement, and rearrangement, where the observed initial target count N0N_{0} is expected to remain unchanged throughout the interaction. The protocol does not assume N0=1N_{0}=1 and therefore applies to scenes containing multiple instances of the manipulated target.

Interactions that intentionally change the target-instance count, such as cutting, splitting, assembly, or disassembly, fall outside the current formulation because the expected target count can change as part of successful task execution. Evaluating such tasks would require an instruction-conditioned expected count rather than a fixed initial-state reference.

MLR is also deliberately specific to target-instance consistency. Count-preserving failures, such as identity drift, deformation, or other changes that preserve the number of detected target instances, are not captured by MLR. These failures constitute a complementary form of temporal inconsistency and motivate the cross-frame supervision introduced by TIA.

A.3 Robustness and Sensitivity Analysis of MLR

Because MLR is derived from automatic target counts, we examine its robustness to evaluation-time detection errors, robot-induced occlusion, and the temporal-persistence criterion. The final protocol combines spatial merging, occlusion-aware handling of under-counts, and temporal persistence, with all detector, query, and evaluation settings fixed across models.

Detector and occlusion robustness.

Spatial merging suppresses redundant detections of the same target, while the occlusion check prevents robot-induced under-counts from being misclassified as target disappearance. Only under-counts are eligible for the occlusion exemption; over-counts are always retained as duplication evidence. An occlusion-supported under-count is treated as non-violating and resets temporal persistence, whereas a target that remains missing after the robot occluder moves away again provides disappearance evidence.

Table 10 contrasts the raw count-deviation rate with the final MLR protocol. The substantial difference between raw detector deviations and the final event rate illustrates the importance of spatial merging, occlusion-aware filtering, and temporal persistence rather than treating every frame-level count mismatch as a physical-consistency failure.

Temporal persistence.

For each eligible video, we record whether an adjusted count deviation N~t​(x)≠N0​(x)\widetilde{N}_{t}(x)\neq N_{0}(x) persists for at least kk consecutive sampled timestamps; k=2k{=}2 is the default MLR rule. This persistence requirement suppresses isolated detector fluctuations while retaining sustained target duplication or disappearance.

Figure 8 reports the persistence length and cumulative onset of occlusion-aware target-instance consistency violations across models. The sole violation under EVEWorld is confined to short persistence lengths, whereas violations in the general I2V baselines extend to larger kk.

Sensitivity to occlusion and persistence thresholds.

The main protocol sets τocc=0.15\tau_{\mathrm{occ}}=0.15, motivated by prior amodal-segmentation protocols that use approximately 15–17% occluded-area criteria to identify nontrivial occlusion (Xiao et al., 2021; Zeng et al., 2022; Zhan et al., 2024), and by target-normalized inter-instance occlusion reasoning in robotic manipulation (Wada et al., 2018).

We recompute MLR on the same shared set 𝒰63\mathcal{U}_{63} with τocc∈{0.10,0.15,0.20,0.25}\tau_{\mathrm{occ}}\in\{0.10,0.15,0.20,0.25\} and k∈{1,2,3}k\in\{1,2,3\}, while keeping all generated videos, detections, tracks, masks, queries, and eligible items fixed. Across all configurations, EVEWorld maintains a lower MLR than Standard SFT, with relative reductions ranging from 70.0% to 88.9%. Under the main setting, MLR decreases from 7/637/63 (11.11%11.11\%) to 1/631/63 (1.59%1.59\%), corresponding to an 85.7% relative reduction.

Lower τocc\tau_{\mathrm{occ}} exempts more under-counts as robot-supported occlusions, whereas larger τocc\tau_{\mathrm{occ}} retains more under-counts as MLR candidates; increasing kk removes short-lived deviations. Neither change reverses the comparison between Standard SFT and EVEWorld.

A.4 Cross-Model Evaluation of MLR

We apply the same occlusion-aware MLR protocol across model families on DreamGenBench. For the controlled cross-model comparison, all event labels are evaluated on the same shared set of 63 detector-eligible items. Table 12 reports event counts, eligible counts, 95% Wilson confidence intervals, and coverage.

Across the evaluated model families, MLR ranges from 7.94–28.57%; CogVideoX1.5, Wan2.2-TI2V, Cosmos-Predict2, and pretrained GigaWorld-0 reach 28.57%, 17.46%, 14.29%, and 12.70%, respectively. These results show that persistent target-instance consistency failures occur across multiple video-generation and embodied-world-model families rather than being specific to Standard SFT or the GigaWorld backbone. On the same shared evaluation set, EVEWorld attains an MLR of 1.59%.

A.5 Cross-Domain Evaluation of MLR

We further evaluate the same occlusion-aware MLR protocol on WorldArena 1.0 (Shang et al., 2026a) using the officially released evaluation code locally. An instruction-only parser first selects manipulation prompts with an identifiable target (817 of 1,000), after which we apply the same initial-frame eligibility rule and MLR protocol used on DreamGenBench.

Table 13 reports the same cross-domain comparison as main-text Table 3, on the shared set of 157 detector-eligible videos and with 95% Wilson confidence intervals for every MLR value. MLR decreases from 27.39% under Standard SFT to 13.38% under EVEWorld, showing that the reduction in persistent target-instance consistency failures extends beyond the DreamGen domain. On this shared set the two baselines coincide at 27.39% while violating on different videos.

A.6 Optional VLM Evaluation

For settings where a capable multimodal model is available, VLM-based temporal reasoning can provide an optional review of detector-based MLR events. This review is auxiliary: it neither replaces nor modifies the frozen detector-based MLR protocol, nor does it change the MLR labels or values reported in this paper. Because VLMs differ in visual and temporal reasoning capability, their judgments are treated as supporting evidence rather than ground truth, with manual review for ambiguous cases. Our qualitative distortion analysis uses the same framework with additional manual verification; examples are provided in Appendix F.3.

VLM Inputs and Outputs.

When reviewing the same evaluation set, the eligible set 𝒟+\mathcal{D}^{+}, target query q⁡(c)q(c), and initial target count N0N_{0} are inherited from the frozen primary MLR protocol. The VLM can be provided with the conditioning frame, instruction, target query, N0N_{0}, frames aligned with the MLR sampling timeline, and a denser temporal view of the rollout. A JSON schema can constrain the output, including event type, interval, supporting frames, visibility explanation, and confidence.

MLR Judgment.

For each candidate event, the VLM reviews the temporal evidence and returns the structured judgment above. Duplication and disappearance are mapped back to the fixed MLR sampling timeline and counted only when they satisfy the original persistence rule. Benign visibility loss, including supported robot or non-robot occlusion, temporary out-of-view motion, cropping, or other temporally supported visibility changes, is flagged as potential false positives of the primary detector-based MLR protocol and reported separately; they do not alter the primary MLR values. Distortion is excluded from MLR because the target count is preserved, but retained as a separate cross-frame consistency failure. Uncertain cases can be passed to manual review, with repeated judgments or a refutation query optionally used to check decision stability.

Appendix B Method Details

B.1 IGR Construction

IGR constructs a corrupted–clean training pair from each valid target trajectory. An offline language parser extracts the target, source, and destination from the instruction. GroundingDINO (Liu et al., 2024a) localizes the target in sampled frames, and temporal association links valid detections into a trajectory. IGR then extracts an instance patch pp and pastes one additional target instance (Ghiasi et al., 2021) at a location Ω\Omega that stays inside the frame, does not overlap the tracked target, and passes the occupancy and collision gates. If no valid paste region exists, we use the clean video as both input and target. With xx the clean video, the corrupted input and the restoration target are

x~=Paste⁡(x,p,Ω),z=VAE⁡(x),z~=VAE⁡(x~).\tilde{x}=\mathrm{Paste}(x,p,\Omega),\qquad z=\mathrm{VAE}(x),\qquad\tilde{z}=\mathrm{VAE}(\tilde{x}). (15)

The model receives z~\tilde{z} and reconstructs zz. We use the final v4 restoration-region annotation shown in Figure 9 to define a binary spatial emphasis mask MrestM_{\mathrm{rest}}. The mask covers the target trajectory and task-relevant interaction regions around the source, destination, robot arm, and gripper, and additionally includes the actual pasted-instance region. Let

M(p)=𝕀[p∈ℛv4∪ℛpaste],M(p)=\mathbb{I}\!\left[p\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{v4}}\cup\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{paste}}\right], (16)

where pp indexes a spatiotemporal latent location. Before normalization, we define

W⁡(p)=1+2​M​(p),W(p)=1+2M(p), (17)

so that restoration-related locations receive three times the reconstruction weight of ordinary locations. We then normalize the map to unit mean,

W^​(p)=W⁡(p)1|Ωlat|​∑q∈ΩlatW⁡(q),\hat{W}(p)=\frac{W(p)}{\frac{1}{|\Omega_{\mathrm{lat}}|}\sum_{q\in\Omega_{\mathrm{lat}}}W(q)}, (18)

where Ωlat\Omega_{\mathrm{lat}} denotes all spatiotemporal locations in the latent grid. This normalization preserves the 3:13{:}1 relative weighting while keeping the global loss scale unchanged.

For DreamGen training, we propose copy–paste corruption with probability pdup=0.5p_{\mathrm{dup}}=0.5. A proposal is applied only when the target trajectory and paste region pass the localization, occupancy, and collision gates; otherwise the sample falls back to the clean input. Consequently, the realized corrupted-sample fraction is lower than the proposal probability and is determined jointly by pdupp_{\mathrm{dup}} and the feasibility gates.

Spatial-Weight Design Selection.

We compared several spatial-emphasis designs before fixing the final IGR weighting. First, we tested a multi-level map that assigned different relative weights to the target path, destination, vacated foreground, gripper, distractors, and pasted instance, using levels of 0.5/2/3/4/60.5/2/3/4/6. We also tested a simpler 3×3\times mask restricted to the target path and locations. The latter was more sensitive to incomplete localization because restoration errors are not confined to these two geometric regions: they can also occur near the gripper, along the robot-arm motion corridor, and around the source and destination regions.

We therefore refined a broader binary restoration mask while keeping a single emphasis factor. The v1 annotation covers the arm–object interaction region broadly; v2 removes irrelevant background-person regions and tightens the foreground support; and v4 corrects the remaining missed arm regions identified during annotation inspection. Table 14 reports the resulting coverage statistics. In our development comparisons, the multi-level weighting and the binary 3×3\times design yielded comparable average performance. We therefore adopt the simpler v4 binary weighting in the final model: ordinary locations receive relative weight 1, restoration-related locations receive relative weight 3, and the actual pasted-instance region uses the same relative weight 3. This design avoids excessively large local weights while retaining coverage of the regions in which duplicate-restoration errors can arise.

B.2 TIA Alignment

TIA consists of local cross-frame alignment and feature transport at a selected backbone layer ℓ⋆\ell^{\star}. We first describe the alignment mechanism and then the offline consistency probe used to select ℓ⋆\ell^{\star} across different domains and backbones. Throughout this section, ft−=norm⁡(Win​Htℓ⋆)f^{-}_{t}=\mathrm{norm}(W_{\mathrm{in}}H_{t}^{\ell^{\star}}) denotes the projected and ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized feature used for locating and transport, and ft+f^{+}_{t} the ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized refined feature after transport, written f¯ℓ⋆\bar{f}^{\ell^{\star}} in the main text. The two stages use different windows: transport scores are computed over the dense window 𝒞ttr\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{tr}}_{t} centered at the same coordinate for every cell, whereas the consistency loss is supervised over the window 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} centered at the true next-frame location utu_{t}.

Cross-frame alignment and feature transport.

At the selected layer ℓ⋆\ell^{\star}, TIA establishes local target consistency between each pair of adjacent frames (Tang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023; Oquab et al., 2024; Doersch et al., 2023; Karaev et al., 2024). A shared linear layer projects features from both frames into a normalized dd-dimensional space. The feature at the previous target location ut−1u_{t-1} then queries the local window 𝒞ttr\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{tr}}_{t} centered at the same coordinate in frame tt, which yields the pre-transport similarity:

st,v−=ft−1−​(ut−1)⊤​ft−​(v).s^{-}_{t,v}=f^{-}_{t-1}(u_{t-1})^{\top}f^{-}_{t}(v). (19)

For feature transport, we apply the local matcher densely. Each cell in frame t−1t{-}1 queries a local window centered at the same coordinate in frame tt; a softmax with temperature τ\tau converts the similarities into transport weights (van den Oord et al., 2018). The projected frame-(t−1)(t{-}1) features are splatted into frame tt using these weights, normalized per cell by the accumulated mass, and written back through a bounded residual update:

Ht′=Htℓ⋆+γ​tanh⁡(Wout​(H¯t−Win​Htℓ⋆)),H_{t}^{\prime}=H_{t}^{\ell^{\star}}+\gamma\,\tanh\!\big(W_{\mathrm{out}}\big(\bar{H}_{t}-W_{\mathrm{in}}H_{t}^{\ell^{\star}}\big)\big), (20)

where H¯t\bar{H}_{t} is the transported feature field, γ\gamma controls the residual magnitude, and WoutW_{\mathrm{out}} is a bias-free linear layer initialized to zero. The first frame is left unchanged. The consistency loss is computed on the refined features after this update: we re-normalize Ht′H_{t}^{\prime} to obtain ft+=norm⁡(Ht′)f^{+}_{t}=\mathrm{norm}(H_{t}^{\prime}), recompute the similarities st,v+=ft−1+​(ut−1)⊤​ft+​(v)s^{+}_{t,v}=f^{+}_{t-1}(u_{t-1})^{\top}f^{+}_{t}(v) over the window 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} centered at the true next-frame location utu_{t}, treat utu_{t} as the positive target and the remaining candidates as negatives, and optimize these correspondences with the temperature-scaled consistency loss ℒTIA\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TIA}} defined in the main text. The transport weights and the consistency loss share the temperature τ\tau but are computed in separate passes.

Layer selection via consistency probing.

We select the TIA attachment layer using an offline consistency probe rather than fixing it heuristically. For each candidate layer, the target feature in the previous frame retrieves its nearest match over the full token grid of the next frame, using the raw ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized block features rather than the WinW_{\mathrm{in}}-projected features used inside TIA, and endpoint error (EPE) (Teed & Deng, 2020) is measured against the localized target position. Because feature reliability can differ across domains and backbone architectures, we additionally report a setting-specific consistency-reliability measure. Table 15 summarizes the probe results and the resulting layer choices for GigaWorld-0/DreamGen, AgiBot, and FlowWAM.

B.3 Joint Training and Inference

The full training objective combines the IGR restoration loss with the TIA consistency loss:

ℒ=ℒIGR+λTIA​ℒTIA.\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IGR}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{TIA}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TIA}}. (21)

For samples with an applied IGR corruption, ℒIGR\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IGR}} restores the clean latent from the count-perturbed input; otherwise, it reduces to the base clean-video training objective. The consistency term is computed on the post-transport features. Its weight and optional noise gate are set per backbone in Appendix C.1.

At inference, the model receives the first frame, the instruction, and the benchmark-specific control input; the parser, the grounder, and the corruption generator are training-time only.

Appendix C Additional Experiments and Analysis

C.1 Implementation Details

Within each evaluation arm, EVEWorld and its control use the same initialization, training set, and optimization budget. The DreamGenBench and EWMBench experiments initialize from GigaWorld-0 Video-Pretrain-2B and update the full transformer with CAME-8bit (Luo et al., 2023), a learning rate of 4.32×10−54.32\times 10^{-5}, and an effective batch size of 64. For DreamGenBench, we train on 92 GR1 videos for 250 steps at 480×768480\times 768 resolution using 93-frame clips at 16 FPS, and evaluate the raw step-250 checkpoint. For EWMBench, we train on 777 AgiBot clips for 50 steps at 480×640480\times 640 resolution with the same frame count and frame rate, and evaluate the raw step-50 checkpoint.

For RoboTwin, both models initialize from the released FlowWAM Stage-1 checkpoint and train a rank-32 LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) on 2,250 episodes for 1,128 optimization steps. We use AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) with a learning rate of 10−410^{-4}, weight decay 0.01, and batch size 8. Training clips contain 29 frames at 24 FPS with a resolution of 480×640480\times 640; evaluation uses the final-epoch checkpoint.

In the evaluated instantiations, TIA uses a 64-dimensional projection, 7×77\times 7 local windows, temperature τ=0.07\tau=0.07, and residual scale γ=0.1\gamma=0.1. It attaches to block 23 on GigaWorld-0 and AgiBot, and block 12 on FlowWAM. On GigaWorld-0, λTIA\lambda_{\mathrm{TIA}} warms from 0 to 0.5 over the first 20 steps and applies at σ∈[0.2,0.5]\sigma\in[0.2,0.5]; FlowWAM uses λTIA=0.1\lambda_{\mathrm{TIA}}=0.1 without noise gating.

DreamGenBench and WorldArena use the raw step-250 checkpoint, 30 denoising steps, and CFG 7.0 at 480×768480\times 768 resolution with 93 frames at 16 FPS. EWMBench uses the raw step-50 checkpoint, the three benchmark seeds, 30 steps, and CFG 7.0 at 480×640480\times 640 with the same clip length and frame rate. RoboTwin uses the final-epoch checkpoint and CFG 5.0 at 480×640480\times 640, generating the full trajectory at 24 FPS. All settings condition on the first frame and instruction; RoboTwin additionally uses robot-only optical flow. Appendix C.4 studies CFG and denoising choices separately.

C.2 IGR Ablation and Duplicate Restoration

Restoration-objective ablation.

Table 16 isolates the effects of duplicate-restoration supervision and spatial weighting. Removing spatial emphasis from the restoration objective still reduces MLR relative to Standard SFT, but leaves substantially more violations than the complete EVEWorld. Conversely, applying spatial emphasis without the duplicate-restoration target does not improve instance consistency. IGR alone reduces MLR to 4.76%, while the complete EVEWorld further reduces it to 1.59%. Notably, removing spatial emphasis yields a slightly higher Overall instruction-following score than the complete model (61.11% vs. 60.85%) but increases MLR from 1.59% to 6.35%, supporting the use of the complete objective.

Controlled duplicate-restoration evaluation.

We further test whether IGR learns to actively correct a corrupted target count rather than merely preserving the input appearance. We construct an independent corruption set by inserting one additional target instance into clean demonstrations and reconstruct the resulting videos under six combinations of paste opacity α\alpha and diffusion noise level σ\sigma. Starting from the Standard SFT checkpoint, the model preserves 92–99% of the injected area, indicating that the spurious instance is largely retained. After 50 IGR fine-tuning steps, retention decreases to 23–42% across all six settings (Table 17). The directional cosine decreases together with retention, showing that the residual reconstruction error becomes not only smaller but also less aligned with the injected duplicate. Figure 10 summarizes both effects across corruption strengths.

Feature diagnostics.

Two additional diagnostics use the same feature-probe family as Appendix B.2. Blocks 25–26 best separate changed from unchanged regions, with score gaps of 0.43–0.45, while blocks 10–16 provide the strongest detection of injected duplicates, with AUC values of 0.79–0.80.

C.3 Evaluation Stability

We quantify variability from repeated instruction-following judgments and inference seeds. Table 18 reruns Gemini-IF on fixed videos and reports every repeat underlying each mean; the main ordering remains unchanged. Table 19 further compares Standard SFT and EVEWorld under matched inference seeds, explicitly controlling for sampling stochasticity. The consistent advantage of EVEWorld indicates that the observed gains are not attributable to favorable seed selection.

Under the transfer protocol, five complete FlowWAM generations from the same checkpoint differ by at most 0.68 Local-11 points (Table 20), indicating stable overall performance across inference seeds. We further examine per-component variation across five inference seeds on a 50-prompt probe set (Table 21). Motion-related metrics show larger variation than appearance-related metrics, but the aggregate Local-11 score remains relatively stable. Local-11 denotes the project-local 11-metric evaluator.

C.4 Training and Long-Horizon Behavior

Training dynamics.

We first examine how instance consistency and instruction following evolve during post-training. As training proceeds toward the selected step-250 checkpoint, MLR generally decreases while Qwen-IF improves, indicating that the reduction in Model Laziness is accompanied by better task fidelity rather than obtained at its expense.

Guidance sensitivity.

We further evaluate classifier-free guidance (CFG) (Ho & Salimans, 2022) across multiple post-training checkpoints and guidance weights. Table 22 shows that stronger guidance generally raises Gemini-IF, but MLR is substantially less monotonic. For example, increasing ww can improve instruction following while leaving MLR unchanged or even increasing it at the same checkpoint. Conversely, the lowest MLR values occur only for particular combinations of training stage and guidance weight rather than systematically at the strongest guidance setting. These results show that CFG primarily controls inference-time instruction fidelity, whereas target-instance consistency remains dependent on the learned post-training behavior.

Long-horizon behavior.

Finally, we examine whether longer rollouts introduce broader physical and process-level degradation. On PBench (NVIDIA, 2025b), overall physical-QA performance decreases as the output duration grows from 3.8 s to 19.8 s, with temporal reasoning degrading most strongly (Table 23). Averaged over all five durations, Standard SFT improves all four PBench dimensions over the pretrained backbone. The advantage becomes more pronounced at longer horizons: over durations of at least 9.8 s, it improves Domain, Phys, and Time by 1.65, 1.95, and 4.24 points on average, respectively. These results indicate that post-training improves broader physical reasoning even as long-horizon generation remains increasingly challenging.

Longer horizons also expose failures that are not captured by target-instance count alone. On 92 matched prompts, both GigaWorld-0 variants exhibit substantially higher shortcut severity, shortcut frequency, and missing-stage frequency at 7.8 s than at 3.8 s (Table 24). At the shared 3.8 s horizon, Wan2.2-TI2V-5B exhibits still larger process errors than either GigaWorld-0 variant. These diagnostics complement MLR by measuring broader failures of process completeness rather than instance consistency alone.

Appendix D Exploration of Alternative Approaches

We evaluate five alternative designs spanning training to inference: PhysicsLatent, EAG, LAD-LoRA, Causal Frontier, and ICH-D. Because their training budgets and generation protocols differ, each route is compared with its own control using the same prompts, conditioning frames, and inference seeds. Table 25 reports MLR and Gemini-IF, with 95% confidence intervals computed by paired bootstrap over the matched pairs.

No alternative jointly reduces MLR and improves instruction following. PhysicsLatent slightly reduces MLR but lowers Gemini-IF, EAG improves Gemini-IF but increases MLR, and the remaining routes show no joint gain.

D.1 PhysicsLatent

PhysicsLatent augments the conditioning sequence with eight learned process tokens. The tokens are computed from the pooled reference-frame latent and prompt embedding and are read by every cross-attention layer. Weak-label heads predict the target’s start and goal boxes, contact events, a coarse 2D trajectory, and the manipulation phase, using pseudo-labels parsed from the instruction together with color and motion heuristics. Against the pretrained 5.8 s control (92 matched pairs), MLR moves from 17.4% to 16.2% while Gemini-IF drops from 45.65 to 40.22, leaving no joint gain.

D.2 EAG

EAG modifies sampling without retraining the video model. After each CFG update, a frozen latent-action model (Schmidt & Jiang, 2024; Ye et al., 2025) assigns a transition energy E⁡(z^0)E(\hat{z}_{0}) to the predicted clean latent z^0\hat{z}_{0} using a soft top-3 aggregation of per-transition reconstruction errors. The sampler then takes one normalized step along the negative energy gradient:

z^0←z^0−w⁡(σ)​‖z^0‖​∇z^0E​(z^0)‖∇z^0E​(z^0)‖,w⁡(σ)=w01+σ,\hat{z}_{0}\leftarrow\hat{z}_{0}\;-\;w(\sigma)\,\|\hat{z}_{0}\|\,\frac{\nabla_{\hat{z}_{0}}E(\hat{z}_{0})}{\|\nabla_{\hat{z}_{0}}E(\hat{z}_{0})\|},\qquad w(\sigma)=\frac{w_{0}}{1+\sigma}, (22)

where w0w_{0} is the guidance weight and w0=0w_{0}{=}0 recovers the unmodified sampler. Against the weight-0 control, Gemini-IF rises from 41.67 to 45.83, while MLR rises from 15.4% to 38.5% (16 prompt–seed pairs, 13 detector-eligible). This small comparison is reported as a development result.

D.3 LAD-LoRA

LAD-LoRA moves the transition-energy signal from sampling to parameter updates. We train a rank-64 attention LoRA (Hu et al., 2022), with the backbone frozen, by adding the energy of the model’s denoised output as a regularizer:

ℒ=ℒEDM+w~1+σ​E​(z^0,θ),\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{EDM}}+\frac{\tilde{w}}{1+\sigma}\,E(\hat{z}_{0,\theta}), (23)

where w~\tilde{w} is recomputed at every step so that the energy gradient stays at a fixed fraction of the denoising gradient on the shared prediction z^0\hat{z}_{0} (target ratio 0.1, capped at 1.0). Against a plain LoRA control under the same protocol (32 matched pairs), LAD-LoRA has the same MLR (3.8%) and reduces Gemini-IF from 51.04 to 47.92.

D.4 Causal Frontier

Causal Frontier generates a video autoregressively in blocks of four latent frames. At each step, the model sees only the clean latents of previously committed blocks, which a near-zero noise level and a mask channel mark as history. The denoising loss applies only to the active block. Generation commits each block irreversibly before denoising the next. At the current budget, prediction errors compound over the rollout (Bengio et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025b): against control50 (16 matched pairs), MLR rises from 30.8% to 41.7% and Gemini-IF falls from 27.08 to 12.50.

D.5 ICH-D

ICH-D applies a learned deletion residual during inference. A frozen linear probe estimates the duplicate probability of each latent cell from novelty and consistency features (16-dimensional statistics collected from several Transformer blocks). A gated residual, whose output projection is initialized to zero and trained before inference, then removes the flagged content from the block-22 representation:

M=sigmoid⁡(β⊤​ϕ​(h)),h22←h22−sigmoid⁡(g)⋅M⊙Wout​(h22),M=\mathrm{sigmoid}\!\big(\beta^{\top}\phi(h)\big),\qquad h_{22}\leftarrow h_{22}-\mathrm{sigmoid}(g)\cdot M\odot W_{\mathrm{out}}(h_{22}), (24)

after which the denoising loop proceeds normally. Over 368 matched pairs against the pretrained model (four seeds), MLR rises from 11.2% to 13.1% and Gemini-IF falls from 45.83 to 31.79; the deletion path introduces its own errors.

Across the matched comparisons, the five alternatives trade off MLR and instruction following, motivating direct restoration and consistency supervision in the backbone.

Appendix E Generalization Results

E.1 Generalization on EWMBench

Table 26 reports all EWMBench components and the official Motion, Semantics, and Overall scores. Relative to Standard SFT, EVEWorld improves Motion by 3.48% and Overall by 1.24%, with a 17.94% gain in DYN. Other components remain close to the matched baseline, with Standard SFT higher on BLEU, Diversity, HSD, and nDTW, and GigaWorld-0 higher on CLIP and Scene. Logic is identical across all three models. The gains of EVEWorld are concentrated in motion-related and aggregate scores rather than uniformly across all EWMBench components.

E.2 FlowWAM Checkpoint Robustness

We evaluate six FlowWAM checkpoints on a fixed RoboTwin slice consisting of episode 45 from each of 50 tasks (Mu et al., 2025). EVEWorld improves PSNR by 2.20–6.22 dB and increases SSIM at every checkpoint (Table 27), showing consistent reference-fidelity gains across checkpoints.

Appendix F Qualitative Results

F.1 Instance Consistency

Figures 11 and 12 provide qualitative examples of target-instance consistency during manipulation. Standard SFT may introduce surplus or missing target instances over the rollout, whereas EVEWorld better maintains target-instance consistency throughout the interaction.

F.2 Cross-Frame Consistency

Figures 13 and 14 compare Standard SFT, IGR-only, and the full EVEWorld at matched stages of the same manipulation. Standard SFT exhibits target duplication during the rollout, and IGR-only can still retain such cross-frame inconsistencies despite directly supervising instance restoration. With TIA added, the full EVEWorld maintains a single coherent target across the corresponding interaction stages. These examples illustrate the complementary roles of IGR and TIA in preserving target consistency over time.

F.3 Target Evolution Comparison

MLR intentionally measures changes in target-instance count and therefore does not capture failures that preserve N0N_{0} while corrupting the target itself. For qualitative analysis, we assess such distortion separately using the same VLM-assisted temporal review framework described in Appendix A.6, supplemented by manual review for a subset of cases. A distortion is marked when the target count remains unchanged but the target undergoes an unsupported change in shape, appearance, or identity that is inconsistent with its preceding temporal state. Figures 15 to 20 show two representative tasks using the same 24 timestamps for all models. In both examples, Standard SFT loses the target and thus produces an MLR count violation, whereas IGR-only preserves the count but progressively distorts the target. EVEWorld preserves both the target count and its cross-frame consistency.

Appendix G Related Work

We group related work into structured embodied world models and physical alignment, object editing, and approaches based on correspondence, tracking, or memory.

Structured embodied world models and physical alignment.

  • •

    4D scene representations. TesserAct extends video generation to jointly predict RGB, depth, and surface normals for 4D scene reconstruction (Zhen et al., 2025). While its richer outputs improve geometric modeling, EVEWorld retains the host model’s native representation and adds post-training restoration supervision for target-instance consistency.

  • •

    Disentangled dynamics. DVG-WM separates a low-resolution dynamics preview from high-fidelity video refinement and evaluates whether the robot acts on the intended object (Shan et al., 2026). Correct target selection, however, does not ensure that the target remains a single consistent instance throughout the interaction; IGR explicitly trains recovery from count-perturbed demonstrations.

  • •

    Object-aware training. DreamX-Phi combines action conditioning and depth prediction with target-mask-weighted reconstruction and relational supervision from a frozen V-JEPA teacher (DreamX Team et al., 2026). TIA adds layer-selected local matching and feature transport for the manipulated target across adjacent frames, while IGR supplies an explicit restoration target when instance consistency is violated.

  • •

    Physics-preference learning. ABot-PhysWorld uses vision-language discriminators to select preferences for physically plausible interaction videos, including contact behavior (Chen et al., 2026b). Its video-level preference signal does not explicitly pair a duplicated target with a clean future; IGR uses that pairing to directly supervise instance-consistent target evolution.

Object editing and corrective supervision.

  • •

    Mask-free video editing. LoVoRA uses learnable localization to add or remove objects in a supplied video from text, without an external mask at inference (Xiao et al., 2025b). IGR instead uses object insertion as a training perturbation; EVEWorld predicts the future from an initial image and instruction without an edit request identifying a spurious target.

  • •

    Effect-aware removal. ROSE removes a specified object and its effects on the scene, including shadows and reflections, from an existing video (Miao et al., 2025). IGR uses the inserted target for a different purpose: restoring the clean manipulation demonstration during post-training, so the world model learns instance consistency before generating future interactions.

Correspondence, tracking, and persistent memory.

  • •

    Joint generation and tracking. Track4Gen jointly learns video generation and point tracking to reduce appearance drift (Jeong et al., 2025). TIA instead selects a layer using target-matching error and locally matches and transports the manipulated target’s features between adjacent frames, directly supervising its cross-frame consistency during generation.

  • •

    Geometry-distilled correspondence. GEM-4D distills dense 4D correspondence from a geometry model into the video backbone, improving geometric consistency without an auxiliary branch at inference (Zhou et al., 2026). TIA focuses its matching and transport on the manipulated target, while IGR adds restoration supervision for instance errors that geometric correspondence alone does not explicitly correct.

  • •

    Scene-revisitation memory. WorldMem stores observations indexed by poses and timestamps to preserve spatial and temporal consistency when a simulated agent revisits a scene (Xiao et al., 2025a). Our evolution supervision instead addresses errors in how the manipulated target changes during an interaction, including unsupported duplication and cross-frame drift.

  • •

    Object-centric memory. SlotMemory organizes key-value features around reusable object slots, improving long-video entity persistence and showing qualitative object-count stability (Dou et al., 2026). IGR complements such persistence by explicitly restoring count-perturbed manipulation videos to supervise instance consistency, rather than relying on stored entity features alone.

  • •

    Manipulation history retrieval. Mem-World uses a 4D surfel memory and action-conditioned history retrieval to maintain scene information under wrist-camera motion and occlusion (Zheng et al., 2026). This historical context complements our direct supervision of the manipulated target: IGR promotes instance consistency, and TIA promotes cross-frame consistency during video prediction.
